title: The call of the king
hookLine: the second week: Christ calls, and you ask to follow closely

lines: SHARE THE HARDSHIP, SHARE THE VICTORY.
NOW TURN THE PICTURE TO CHRIST.
cards: A king stands before his people and makes an offer. He's setting out on a hard campaign. Whoever comes with him will eat what he eats and wear what he wears, work beside him by day and keep watch with him by night.
They'll share the hardship, then the victory. Ignatius of Loyola sets that scene at the start of the second week of his Spiritual Exercises.

He asks the one praying to picture a good leader calling like that, and what a decent person would answer. Then he turns the picture around. If that's how people answer an earthly king, what about Christ?

teach.h: FOLLOW ME. THEY LEFT THEIR NETS.
teach.b: In the Gospels, a call can be very short. Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee, sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men."
Then: "And they straightway left their nets, and followed him." No speech, no terms. Ignatius slows that moment down.

teach.h: SHARE THE WORK, SHARE THE GLORY.
teach.b: In his meditation, Christ the king calls the whole world, and each person one by one, to share his work and his hardship, so as to share his glory. Anyone with judgment, Ignatius says, would offer themselves for the work.
But some will want to offer more: to follow Christ even in bearing wrongs and in poverty, if that's where he leads.

teach.h: THE BIG ANSWER IS A REQUEST.
teach.b: That bigger answer isn't a boast. It's a request.

teach.h: KNOW HIM, LOVE HIM, FOLLOW HIM.
teach.b: From here on, the grace Ignatius has people ask for runs close to this: to know Jesus more from the inside, to love him more, and to follow him more closely. Know, love, follow, in that order.

It's hard to follow someone you've only heard about, so next come gospel stories: the birth, the hidden years, the baptism, the calls by the lake. The one praying watches Jesus up close before deciding anything.
An old English prayer, which tradition gives to Richard of Chichester, asks to see him more clearly, love him more dearly, and follow him more nearly. Today's line borrows its end.
Following more nearly isn't a leap into heroics. It's one step closer than yesterday.

how: In the Spiritual Exercises, the meditation on the call of the king opens the second week; retreatants then pray through gospel scenes of Jesus' life, asking to know, love and follow him more closely.

games.q: what does “the call of the king” mean?
o: a medieval ceremony where knights swore loyalty to their ruler
the prophet Samuel anointing young David as Israel's next king
Ignatius' meditation on Christ calling each person to share his work

p: calls companions to share the hardship
know him, love him, follow him
the end of an old English prayer

s: Ignatius' meditation is really about an earthly ruler
he starts with a good earthly king only to turn the picture to Christ.
in Matthew, Simon and Andrew leave their nets straightway
"and they straightway left their nets, and followed him."
in the second week, following comes before knowing
know, love, follow, in that order. it's hard to follow well someone you've only heard about.

games.q: in Ignatius' meditation, the king calls companions to share his hardship and then his victory. what answer is Ignatius hoping for?
o: say it sounds good, and stay home.
offer to work, and ask to follow more closely still.
wait for the victory, then join.
games.why: Ignatius says anyone with judgment would offer to work. the more generous answer asks to follow even more closely, wherever that leads.

practice: Stand by the lake, a wet net in your hands, and hear the call, short and plain. Notice what rises, eagerness, hesitation, a list of reasons this isn't a good time, and don't fix any of it.
If you pray, ask in your own words to know him more, love him more, and follow him more nearly; if you don't, notice one thing you'd want to move a step closer to.

wordCard.voice: The call of the king. Ignatius' meditation that opens the second week: Christ calls each person to share his work, and the generous answer asks to follow him more closely.

carryVoice: Your line: to follow more nearly. Know first, then love, then follow. That's today, done.
